extracted.intended_audience: junior scholars and academic grant applicants (and grant reviewers/panelists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria used by fellowship/ grant panelists in the humanities, history, and social sciences for judging proposals, applicants, and supporting materials; covers formal criteria (clarity, originality, significance, methods, feasibility, quality) and informal/evanescent signals (letters, prestige, elegance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of evidence considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists base judgments on the proposal (project description, bibliography, timetable), information about the applicant (bio sketch, personal statement, CV, publications, transcripts, teaching), supporting material (letters of recommendation), and screeners' comments and rankings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These evidence types receive different weight (the proposal typically counts much more than the letters). Panelists treat the dossier as a genre and compare across applications using these standard elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to proposal genre and conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals are expected to follow recognizable genre conventions (e.g., the first paragraph should ‘make it clear what’s going on’ and proposals should discuss the project’s significance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to adhere to these conventions often dooms a proposal regardless of intrinsic interest. Panelists read quickly and use conventions as a basis for rapid assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity (writing and argumentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity defined variously as luminescence, transparency, precision, analytical articulation, crispness, and tightness of prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity is often the first criterion mentioned and is a sine qua non for excellence. Because reviewers face time constraints, unclear or boring writing leads to deselection. Clear prose signals clear thinking, competence, and careful drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality / Craftsmanship / Depth / Thoroughness
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality is a catch-all encompassing craftsmanship, depth, attention to detail, thoroughness, rigor, and solidity (scholarly and empirical soundness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality proposals show careful, well-crafted work, depth of engagement, meticulous use of sources, and empirical/scholarly soundness; factual errors or superficial trendiness are grounds for rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality (multidimensional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality includes multiple types: new approach, new data, new theory, new topic, new method, new outcomes, or work in an understudied area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists employ a broader definition of originality than canonical scientific accounts. Humanists/historians tend to emphasize originality of approach and data (new texts/sources), while social scientists emphasize method and a mixture of types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance (scholarly vs social/political)
rubrics_metrics.description: Significance is parsed into scholarly (intellectual/theoretical) significance and social/political significance (giving voice to subordinate groups or producing socially useful knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish significance of topic from significance of impact (on knowledge, on field, on academia, political, social). Panelists overall prioritize academic/knowledge impact more than social/political impact, but emphasis varies by discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods (theory–method–data articulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of methods includes the articulation among theory, method, and data, and the proper use of theory in supporting the research design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods are weighted differently across disciplines; social scientists often privilege rigorous methods (testing hypotheses, formal models), while other styles emphasize attention to empirical complexity and detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility (readiness, track record, plan)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feasibility assesses whether the applicant is well equipped to complete the proposed project, considering readiness, past record, and the work plan/timetable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although some funders instruct reviewers to focus on the proposal rather than past record, the applicant’s track record and concrete plan influence judgments about feasibility; relative weight can depend on competition (e.g., graduate vs senior).

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters of recommendation — specificity and immersion
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters that matter are those that convey specific information about the project, explain its importance in concrete terms, and demonstrate that the letter-writer has immersed themselves in the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic, hyperbolic, or formulaic letters ('the best in the field') are discounted. Specific descriptions of what the student has done and how skills will influence the project gain attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters of recommendation — prestige and signaling
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters function as a signal: the stature or fame of the letter-writer can influence evaluators regardless of substantive content (halo effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some panelists pay more attention to the writer’s reputation than the letter’s content; this can advantage applicants with access to prestigious networks and may bias outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of letters that influence decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Two types of letters are most influential: (1) letters that explain a project’s importance in specific terms and situate it in the literature; (2) letters from individuals panelists know or regard as having intellectual integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both content-rich letters and letters from trusted, well-known scholars can create persuasive evidence; the combination of strong letters plus a great proposal helps build consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impression management and the 'bullshit penalty'
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal-writing involves a degree of impression management or overstating certainty; panelists may impose a 'bullshit penalty' on proposals that seem shallow or formulaic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some impression management is unavoidable, authenticity of intellectual engagement should shine through; formulaic optimism can be penalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advanced/project maturity advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects that are well advanced are often judged favorably because they are more specific, complete, and 'elegant'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists may fund advanced projects as a 'reward for doing the work' even when that conflicts with programmatic goals (e.g., supporting early-stage fieldwork).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-pressure-driven deselection behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Because reviewers process many applications under time constraints and with little compensation, they tend to deselect poorly written or boring proposals rather than actively search for the best ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the proposal easy to read and immediately engaging; unclear or laborious prose reduces chances of being seriously considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemological style influences (constructivist, comprehensive, positivist, utilitarian)
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists invoke different epistemological styles that shape what they value: constructivist (knowledge for social change; personal/political elements), comprehensive (knowledge for knowledge’s sake; informed rationale), positivist (generalize, disprove theories, formal models), utilitarian (solve real-world problems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three-quarters of panelists favored the comprehensive style; choice of style affects weighting among originality, methods, and significance. Awareness of likely panel epistemological leanings can inform framing of proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evanescent applicant qualities (excitement, elegance, cultural capital, moral authenticity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal qualities tied to the applicant—such as generating excitement, appearing elegant/intelligent, displaying cultural capital, and showing moral authenticity/commitment—shape judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These informal signals are valued by many panelists and can advantage applicants who can effectively convey excitement and intellectual commitment beyond the written plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary variation in weighting
rubrics_metrics.description: Different disciplines and disciplinary clusters assign different weights to criteria (e.g., originality may be more heavily weighted than feasibility overall; historians/humanists prioritize intellectual significance and approach/data originality; social scientists emphasize method).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no single integrated disciplinary hierarchy—successful proposals should be framed to align with the evaluative emphases common in the target discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical and factual accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals must be empirically and factually sound; factual errors, anachronisms, or incorrect assumptions lead to rapid elimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accuracy is part of 'quality' and is non-negotiable; attention to primary sources and correct factual framing is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of screeners and preliminary rankings
rubrics_metrics.description: Screeners’ comments and preliminary rankings are part of the dossier and influence panel discussion and decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should be aware that early-stage screening affects later deliberations; clarity and concise presentation help screeners form favorable initial impressions.
